mine: the Canaanite, the king of Arad
note: Hebrew melekh-'Arad is "king of Arad"; Arad is a Negev city (cf. 33:40, Josh 12:14), not the king's personal name.

kjv: by the way of the spies
note: Hebrew ha'atarim is most likely a place or route name; the KJV, following the Targum, read it as tarim "spies" (cf. 14:6).
Hebrew haqqeloqel means contemptible, miserable (from qalal "be light, trifling"); the manna is despised, not described as light in texture.

kjv: What he (Yahweh) did in the Red sea, and in the brooks of Arnon
mine: Waheb in Suphah, and the wadis, the Arnon
note: Hebrew 'et-Vahev beSufah is an obscure poetic fragment, now usually taken as a place name Waheb in a district Suphah; the KJV follows a Jewish tradition reading it as "what he gave at the Sea of Reeds". Context: place names (medium confidence). The object marker 'et with no verb shows a quoted fragment. Waheb and Suphah are best taken as places, matching 'the wadis of the Arnon' and the itinerary of 21:10-20. ESV, NASB, NRSV and NJPS read 'Waheb in Suphah'; NIV 'Zahab in Suphah'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'what he did at the Red Sea' (Suphah taken as Yam Suph) — Targum, Rashi, Vulgate (sicut fecit in mari Rubro), KJV; (2) 'he set Zoob on fire', reading a verb — LXX; (3) 'Zahab' rather than 'Waheb' — NIV, following some versional evidence.

kjv: by the direction of the lawgiver
note: Hebrew bimchoqeq means "with a ruler's staff" (instrument, parallel to "with their staffs"); the KJV takes the participle as a person, "lawgiver".
Hebrew hayshimon "the desert/wasteland" has the article and may be a common noun; the KJV treats it as a place name.
